previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of systolic heart failure (EF 30%), atrial fibrillation, diabetes, and obesity was admitted for chest discomfort and shortness of breath. The chest pain was burning, non-exertional, and resolved with club soda, with stable troponins and no EKG changes, ruling out acute coronary syndrome. The symptoms were attributed to GERD or musculoskeletal causes, possibly triggered by alcohol. He had acute on chronic systolic heart failure exacerbation due to fluid overload, likely from dietary indiscretion and medication noncompliance. He was treated with IV Lasix, then transitioned to oral torsemide, resulting in an 18-pound weight loss and symptom improvement. During admission, he developed right foot cellulitis with a fluid collection, which was drained at bedside twice; wound culture grew MSSA, and he completed a course of vancomycin with a planned two-week course of oral dicloxacillin. Due to chronically unstable INR and a CHADS score of 5, he was transitioned from warfarin to Pradaxa. His insulin dose was reduced due to hypoglycemia, and plans were made to consider switching to glargine. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged for podiatry, primary care, and colonoscopy for reported maroon stools.

radiology_notes.text:
CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with new stroke.

STUDY:  MRI head without and with contrast, MRA head without contrast and MRA
neck with contrast.

COMPARISON STUDY:  CT head dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal T1, axial T1, T2, FLAIR, gradient echo and
diffusion-weighted images were obtained of the brain prior to administration
of contrast.  Axial T1 and sagittal MP-RAGE images were obtained after
administration of contrast with axial and coronal reconstructions.  3D TOF MR
angiography of the head was obtained without administration of contrast.  MR
angiography of the neck was done after administration of contrast using bolus
tracking technique.  Multiplanar reconstructions were performed.

FINDINGS:

MRI HEAD:  An area of slow diffusion is noted in the left medial temporal lobe
with associated FLAIR hyperintensity.  This is suggestive of an early subacute
infarct in left posterior cerebral artery territory.  There is no evidence of
hemorrhagic transformation of infarct.  On post-contrast images there is
gyriform enhancement of this area.

An area of encephalomalacia was seen in the right parietal lobe which likely
represents sequelae of old infarct.

Brainstem and cerebellum appear normal.  Ventricles, cortical sulci and
extra-axial CSF spaces are normal.  The major intracranial flow voids are
maintained.

Polyps/retention cyst is noted in the left maxillary sinus.  Visualized
mastoid air cells are clear.  Orbits are unremarkable.

MRA HEAD:  Arteries of the anterior circulation including bilateral
intracranial internal carotid arteries, anterior and middle cerebral arteries
appear normal. Small infundibuli are noted at the origins of posterior
communicating artery and anterior choroidal artery in bilateral internal
carotid arteries. Arteries of posterior circulation including bilateral
vertebral arteries, basilar artery and posterior cerebral arteries appear
normal.  There is no evidence of stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm greater than
3 mm.

MRA NECK:  Three-vessel aortic arch is noted.  The origin of great vessels
appear normal.  The origin of right vertebral artery is normal.  

There is loss of signal in proximal left subclavian and proximal part of left
vertebral artery which is likely artefactual. However, narrowing at this level
cannot be completely excluded.

Bilateral common carotid artery, internal and external carotid arteries appear
normal.  Bilateral vertebral arteries are patent.

There is no evidence of stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm greater than 3 mm.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Early subacute infarct in the right medial temporal lobe and occipital
lobe (left posterior cerebral artery territory).
2.  Encephalomalacia in right parietal lobe which is likely a sequela of old
infarct.
3.  No evidence of stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm greater than 3 mm in
arteries of head.
4. There is loss of signal in proximal left subclavian and proximal part of
left vertebral artery which is likely artefactual. However, narrowing at this
level cannot be completely excluded.
